caption:
From robotics to drones to training autonomous vehicles through Mario Kart, UMD researchers are aiming to #DoGoodUMD through AI. 

Take a tour through just a few of our #AIMaryland projects:

RoboScout DTC (@umdclarkschool): These Scout robots are designed to identify and triage injuries so first responders can better care for those in need.

Perception and Robotics (@marylandroboticscenter): A pair of specialized drones, one of which can autonomously navigate emergency obstacles while the other can be used for agricultural monitoring.

S3AM Oyster Drone (@umdclarkschool, @umd_agnr, @umdscience): This custom underwater drone navigates the Chesapeake floor to support precision oyster aquaculture. 

Mario Kart Machine Learning (@umdaerospace): An AI system trained to drive Mario Kart tracks and prioritize safety, which can then make future self-driving vehicles safer. 

FoodSecureDMV: A voice bot that prompts anyone experiencing food insecurity to help them access resources while taking into account a variety of factors. 

GenAI Architecture (@umdmappschool): GenAI can turn a hand-drawn image into a photorealistic design concept to assist designers with brainstorming, efficiency, and enriching conversation. 

SMART Lab Calico: This miniature wearable system performs a variety of tasks to assist the visually impaired.

Another #UMDHomecoming in the books 🐢 

From a full week of events to Halloween fun and Homecoming Saturday, it was a fall weekend full of of Maryland pride in College Park 💛 

More At the link in our bio!

caption:
Great teachers never stop learning. This Terp team’s new AI module helps teachers learn, grow and support their students’ success. 

Using recordings and transcripts of lessons, the artificial intelligence delivers personalized support for both educators and students, offering much more frequent feedback than previous methods. UMD researchers spanning @umdcollegeofed, @infocollegeumd, and @umdclarkschool partnered to develop this AI model that analyzes information in collaboration with a certified education coach.

Typically, educators receive feedback only once or twice a year, but the M-Powering Teachers program offers ongoing support for continuous learning. By integrating educational theory, machine learning, language processing, field experiments, and more, M-Powering Teachers provides a dynamic platform dedicated to enhancing the effectiveness of modern education. #AIMaryland

Read more at the link in our bio!

caption:
Spotted lanternflies are nearly everywhere in Maryland, leaving a sticky mess on cars and plants and crashing your al fresco meals.

But while the eye-catching insect seems to be everywhere, they’re more annoying than a real threat. “Don’t panic. They’re not going to hurt you or hurt your plants. Hang tight, because it’s all going to pass,” said entomology Professor and University of Maryland Extension Specialist Paula Shrewsbury.

Here are some key things you should know about the invasive species:
 🔘 Spotted lanternflies originally arrived in the U.S. in 2014. They have since spread to at least 17 states, including Maryland.
 🔘 Like other invasive species, the population will ebb and flow. Maryland is at the start of a boom period for three to five years, and then the number of spotted lanternflies should dip and level out.
 🔘 Predators are emerging, such as other insects and various birds. 
 🔘 Spotted lanternfly nymphs may gather on small plants, but the adults feed mainly on woody trees without causing much damage. They’re most harmful to grape vines.
 🔘 #UMD researchers are studying a commercially available bio-insecticide that shows strong results as an effective solution to control the spotted lanternfly population and will offer recommendations to Maryland farmers.

Learn more at our link in bio.

caption:
Ryan Collins ’16, MBA ’20 was on his way home from a training ride, the gritty kind that made him feel like he could conquer the world. After spending the past couple of years racing up the ranks from a junior mid-Atlantic cycling champion to one of the top riders in the nation, he’d just received his dream phone call: an invitation to try out for the Olympic training team representing the U.S. in Tokyo. His bags were packed, and he was scheduled to fly out to the camp the next morning.

The next thing he knew, he and his bike were crumpled on the ground as onlookers’ screams pierced the air. In a flash, an approaching car had collided with him head-on.

Paramedics rushed Collins to the hospital, where doctors who recognized the elite athlete in their care reluctantly delivered the news: Not only was he not flying out in the morning to the Olympic training camp, but the odds were that he’d never ride a bike again.

“And I’m thinking, ‘Well, just watch me,’” Collins says. 

Now, nearly a decade after the accident, he's breaking records as an ultracyclist, racing for six to 12 hours at a time and winning national and European championships. 

More on his remarkable journey at the link in our bio!
